explanations.explanation: Sorrow is right, baker. Baruch says, “Woe is me because the LORD has added sorrow to my pain!” (Jeremiah 45:3) So he was already hurting, and he says more got piled on top. I think that's a tired man talking, and the LORD doesn't brush it aside. He quotes Baruch's own words right back to him.

Strength is a nice thought, friend, but it's not what Baruch says. He says the LORD has added sorrow to his pain (Jeremiah 45:3). Nobody groaning “Woe is me” is about to list strength as a complaint. I think a man that worn out would have loved some extra strength.

Courage would be a great thing to add, but that's not Baruch's word. He says, “Woe is me because the LORD has added sorrow to my pain!” (Jeremiah 45:3) The word is sorrow. I think Baruch was running low on courage, and he doesn't say it was added.

True. Baruch says, “I am worn out with groaning and have found no rest.” (Jeremiah 45:3) Those are his words, and the LORD repeats them to him. I think anybody who has lain awake at 3 a.m. knows that feeling. It's honest, and it's right there in the text.

Not quite, baker. The text says Baruch does say it: “I am worn out with groaning and have found no rest.” (Jeremiah 45:3) So the statement is true. The words are Baruch's own, and the LORD speaks them back to him. He says he has found no rest, and that's what the verse records.

Demolish is the word. The LORD says, “Throughout the land I will demolish what I have built and uproot what I have planted.” (Jeremiah 45:4) That's the LORD speaking about what He Himself built and planted. Big words, and the verse doesn't soften them. It's a heavy line, and the passage lets it stand.

Guard sounds friendly, friend, but it's not in the verse. The LORD says, “Throughout the land I will demolish what I have built and uproot what I have planted.” (Jeremiah 45:4) Guarding is what you do to keep something standing. This verse is about what's coming down, and it talks about uprooting too.

Repair is the kind of thing I'd say with a spatula in my hand, baker, but it's not what the verse says. The LORD says, “Throughout the land I will demolish what I have built and uproot what I have planted.” (Jeremiah 45:4) Demolish is the word, and it goes with uproot. Those two words are about taking down, not fixing up.

Great things for himself is right. The LORD asks, “But as for you, do you seek great things for yourself?” (Jeremiah 45:5) The question is aimed straight at Baruch, by name. It's a short question, and I think it lands hard. The text doesn't say what those great things were, so I'll leave that open too.

Revenge is a strong guess, friend, but the text never mentions it. The LORD asks, “But as for you, do you seek great things for yourself?” (Jeremiah 45:5) Enemies don't come up anywhere in these five verses. The question is about Baruch and the great things he seeks for himself.

Good guess, since Jeremiah is the one speaking to Baruch, but it's not in the text. The LORD asks, “But as for you, do you seek great things for yourself?” (Jeremiah 45:5) Praise from Jeremiah never comes up. The question is about great things for himself.
Careful, baker, this one flips on you. The LORD doesn't say keep reaching. He says, “Stop seeking!” (Jeremiah 45:5) He asks the question first, then tells Baruch to stop. So the statement is false.

False is right. The LORD asks, “But as for you, do you seek great things for yourself? Stop seeking!” (Jeremiah 45:5) That's the opposite of keep reaching. It's a short command, and the text doesn't add anything to it. The LORD speaks it to Baruch directly.

Every living creature is right. The LORD says, “For I will bring disaster on every living creature, declares the LORD.” (Jeremiah 45:5) That's a wide net, and the verse doesn't narrow it down. It's a heavy line, and I won't joke about it.

Judah's officials aren't named here, friend. The LORD says, “For I will bring disaster on every living creature, declares the LORD.” (Jeremiah 45:5) That covers far more than one group. The verse says every living creature, and that's all it says about who.

False prophets are a reasonable guess for a prophetic book, baker, but they don't show up in these verses. The LORD says, “For I will bring disaster on every living creature, declares the LORD.” (Jeremiah 45:5) No group is picked out. The words are every living creature.

Life is right. The LORD says, “…wherever you go, I will grant your life as a spoil of war.” (Jeremiah 45:5) After the heavy news, that's what Baruch is promised. A spoil of war is what a person carries away from the fight. It's his life, and the LORD is the one who grants it.

Land is a natural guess, friend, since land is all over verse 4. But the promise to Baruch is different. The LORD says, “…wherever you go, I will grant your life as a spoil of war.” (Jeremiah 45:5) It says wherever you go, so I think the promise travels with him. What he's granted is his life.

A name is a fine thing to have, baker. I got mine carved on a handle, after all. But the verse says something else: “…wherever you go, I will grant your life as a spoil of war.” (Jeremiah 45:5) The LORD grants Baruch his life. His name isn't mentioned there.
